title: Initiative Econometrics: Prioritization Index for Cycle-aware Roadmapping
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem: Traditional RICE/RoI exercises at Redwood capture impact and confidence but underweight operational economics (latency/cost elasticity) and cycle timing. Goal: create a reproducible, quantitative rubric — Initiative Econometrics Index (IEI) — that blends expected customer value, OKR alignment, latency/cost elasticity, rollout friction, and cycle timing into one comparable score.

Why it matters to Redwood: product teams frequently decide between lower-latency runtime improvements, Dedicated capacity features, and Console UX work. Those initiatives have different unit economics and different time-to-value within a sprint cycle. IEI will help prioritize initiatives so that the roadmap better balances cost-per-token improvements, user-facing latency wins, and enterprise readiness work while remaining cycle-aware.

Core components (scoring inputs):
- Expected Value (EV): qualitative->quantitative translation of expected revenue/retention/engagement impact (0-100).
- OKR Alignment Multiplier (OAM): 0.5x-1.5x factor based on alignment to company/quarter OKRs.
- Latency/Cost Elasticity (LCE): a composite score capturing how much user behavior or unit cost changes per 10ms latency or 1% cost change. Expressed as 0-100 with directionality encoded in sign.
- Rollout Friction (RF): integration, infra, and compliance friction cost (0-100) that reduces score.
- Cycle Timing Bonus (CTB): discrete bonus for initiatives that can be completed in the current cycle (e.g., +10) vs multi-cycle (-5) to penalize long runway for quick experiments.

Scoring formula (proposed): IEI = ((EV * OAM) + LCE) * (1 - RF/200) + CTB.

Deliverables: rubric docs, an interactive spreadsheet with example scoring for 30 current initiatives, a lightweight web UI (not gated) for PMs to score initiatives, and integration guidelines for the roadmap board so IEI can be used as a sortable field.

How it differs from RICE: IEI explicitly models operational elasticity (latency/cost) and cycle scheduling effects instead of only Reach/Impact/Confidence/Effort. This makes it more actionable for platform trade-offs where unit economics matter as much as surface-level user metrics.
decisions: Weight EV as primary driver but cap OAM at 1.5x to avoid single-OKR dominance.
Represent LCE with signed values to reflect negative elasticity (cost increases hurt) or positive (small latency wins yield disproportionate engagement gains).
Use RF as a dampening factor (0-100) that halves impact at RF=100 to reflect heavy regulatory/infra cost.
Apply CTB only when cycle estimate <= cycle capacity to prevent gaming by artificially breaking work into smaller tickets.
acceptance_criteria: IEI rubric documented in Confluence with worked examples for runtime, Dedicated, and Console initiatives.
Interactive scoring spreadsheet with formulas and comments published and shared with PM/Engineering leads.
Scored 30 live initiatives across custodial teams and validated ranking with at least 3 stakeholder reviews.
Roadmap board field created and synced; IEI visible as a sortable column for next planning session.
Playbook entry: how to handle cross-team dependencies and tie-break rules for tied IEI scores.

risks: Elasticity estimates are noisy and may bias towards initiatives with more telemetry; require calibration safeguards.
Stakeholder buy-in risk: platform teams may see numeric scores as prescriptive; include qualitative override rules.
Data dependencies: missing historical cost/latency data for some private deployment customers could skew LCE.
Over-optimization risk: teams may game CTB by slicing work; governance needed.
notes: Prototype must remain editable by PMs; do not lock formula cells in spreadsheet until after calibration.
Consider a later extension: map IEI to suggested rollout strategy (canary/AB/manual fallback) based on RF and LCE.
If successful, IEI will be proposed as an input to the quarterly planning rubric and resourcing conversations.
